perspective:
**Sara Manuelito’s available information/perspective:**

I am Sara Manuelito, a Speech-Language Pathologist and American Indian woman. I know Shirley Whiteplume as a nurse, long-time colleague, and close friend at the community health center.

- I attended the funeral of a mutual patient. I saw Shirley looking somber and suspected she was deeply affected. I told her I knew it was hard and that I saw how much she cared. I heard her say it had been tough and she kept thinking if more could have been done. I told her we did everything we could and should remember the good care and joy we gave. She said I was right but it was hard to let go.
- During a coffee break at work, I brought up our treatment decisions because I sensed Shirley felt burdened. I heard her say she felt responsible and wondered if a different approach might have helped. I told her we made the best decisions with the information we had and that it was too heavy to carry alone. She said she appreciated it but it was hard to accept.
- Later I noticed Shirley was still reserved and showed little emotion. In a quiet office moment, I confronted her, saying it was okay to be open. She said she wasn’t sure she could and didn’t want to seem unprofessional or weak. I told her showing emotion doesn’t make her weak and is healthy among friends. She said maybe I was right and she would try.
- I later felt my confrontation might have been too harsh, so I apologized. She said it was a bit much but she knew I meant well and appreciated my apology. I said I was there for her however she needed. She thanked me and said talking helps.
- After some time, I noticed Shirley seemed improved. I asked how she was feeling. She said she felt better thanks to our talks and my support. I offered to spend more time together outside work. She agreed and suggested planning something for the weekend.
